summary: Psalm 111 begins with public thanksgiving and then names why Yahweh is to be praised: his works are great, remembered, gracious, just, and enduring. The psalm moves from God’s provision and covenant faithfulness to the trustworthiness of his precepts, ending with wisdom, understanding, and lasting praise.
whyItMatters: This short psalm gathers several major concerns of Book V of Psalms: remembered works, covenant, reverence, and praise. Its alphabetic acrostic form gives ordered shape to a wide-ranging meditation on Yahweh’s character and deeds.

context.author: No individual author is named in the chapter. Psalms is an anthology with many writers and collections, and authorship claims for individual psalms should be handled cautiously when not stated in the text.
context.audience: Israel’s worshiping and instructed community, with later Jewish and Christian communities also receiving these poems for public prayer and private life.
context.date: Individual psalms may preserve material from the monarchy through the postexilic period; assigning one date to the whole Psalter, or to this psalm from this chapter alone, would be misleading.
context.setting: The psalm speaks in the council of the upright and in the congregation, using public praise language rather than narrating a single dated event.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew praise poetry. Psalm 111 is an alphabetic acrostic, though that structure is mostly invisible in ordinary English translation.

outline.heading: Wholehearted public praise
outline.note: The speaker begins with praise and thanks to Yahweh among the upright and the congregation.

outline.heading: Great works remembered
outline.note: Yahweh’s works are described as great, worthy of pondering, majestic, righteous, memorable, gracious, and merciful.

outline.heading: Provision and inheritance
outline.note: The psalm says Yahweh gives food to those who fear him, remembers his covenant, and shows his people power by giving them the heritage of the nations.

outline.heading: Trustworthy precepts
outline.note: Yahweh’s works and precepts are described with truth, justice, certainty, permanence, and uprightness.

outline.heading: Redemption, wisdom, and praise
outline.note: The psalm closes by naming redemption, covenant, God’s holy and awesome name, the fear of Yahweh as wisdom’s beginning, and enduring praise.

keyVerses.text: Yahweh’s works are great, pondered by all those who delight in them.
keyVerses.why: This line states the psalm’s main subject: Yahweh’s works and the human response of attentive delight.

keyVerses.text: He has given food to those who fear him. He always remembers his covenant.
keyVerses.why: This verse joins provision with covenant memory, two central claims in the middle of the psalm.

keyVerses.text: He has sent redemption to his people. He has ordained his covenant forever. His name is holy and awesome!
keyVerses.why: This verse gathers redemption, covenant, and reverence for Yahweh’s name into one concentrated statement.

keyVerses.text: The fear of Yahweh is the beginning of wisdom. All those who do his work have a good understanding. His praise endures forever!
keyVerses.why: The final verse turns the psalm’s praise into wisdom language and ends where the chapter began: with praise.

themes: the fear of Yahweh and wisdom

questions.question: Who is speaking in this psalm?
questions.answer: The psalm uses an individual voice: “I will give thanks to Yahweh with my whole heart.” That personal praise is not private only, because it happens “in the council of the upright, and in the congregation.” The chapter presents one worshiper’s thanks as part of a gathered community’s praise.

questions.question: What does “Praise Yah!” mean here?
questions.answer: “Praise Yah!” is an opening summons to praise using a shortened form of Yahweh’s name. In this chapter it introduces thanksgiving rather than a narrative scene. The same verse immediately expands the response: the speaker gives thanks to Yahweh with the whole heart.

questions.question: What are “Yahweh’s works” in this psalm?
questions.answer: The chapter does not list one single event in detail. It describes Yahweh’s works as great, honorable, majestic, memorable, powerful, truthful, and just. The psalm gives examples in broad terms: food for those who fear him, covenant remembrance, heritage for his people, and redemption.

questions.question: Does “fear” mean being terrified of Yahweh?
questions.answer: In this psalm, “fear” is tied to covenant life, wisdom, and understanding. Those who fear Yahweh receive food, and “the fear of Yahweh” is called the beginning of wisdom. The word includes reverence and serious regard for God, not casual indifference.

questions.question: What covenant is the psalm talking about?
questions.answer: The psalm says twice that Yahweh remembers or ordains his covenant, but it does not stop to define the covenant in historical detail. Within the chapter, covenant language is connected with provision, redemption, and permanence. A reader should notice the claim without importing a full covenant history from outside the chapter as if the psalm had narrated it here.

questions.question: What does it mean that Yahweh gave “the heritage of the nations”?
questions.answer: The phrase says Yahweh showed his people the power of his works by giving them a heritage connected with the nations. The chapter does not narrate the event or explain all its historical details. Readers commonly connect the wording with Israel’s received land and inheritance traditions, but the psalm itself states the point as evidence of Yahweh’s power toward his people.

questions.question: Are “precepts” the same as Yahweh’s “works”?
questions.answer: The psalm moves from Yahweh’s works to Yahweh’s precepts without treating them as enemies. His works are “truth and justice,” and his precepts are “sure.” The next verse says they are established forever and done in truth and uprightness, so the chapter presents God’s acts and commands as consistent with each other.

questions.question: Why does a praise psalm end by talking about wisdom?
questions.answer: The final verse says “The fear of Yahweh is the beginning of wisdom,” linking praise with a way of understanding and living. The psalm does not treat praise as mere emotion; it connects reverence, doing God’s work, and good understanding. That ending fits the chapter’s movement from remembered works to a wise response.

questions.question: What is special about the form of Psalm 111?
questions.answer: Psalms 111 and 112 are acrostic poems that advance almost line by line through the Hebrew alphabet. That structure is largely hidden in English, but it matters because it gives the poem an ordered shape. The form does not create a secret code; it helps hold together the psalm’s praise of Yahweh’s works, covenant, precepts, and wisdom.

glossary.def: A shortened form of Yahweh’s name, used in the opening call to praise.
A gathered group; in this verse it is paired with “congregation” as the setting where the speaker gives thanks.
A binding relationship or commitment; in this psalm Yahweh remembers it and ordains it forever.
Commands or instructions; the psalm says Yahweh’s precepts are sure and established forever.
Rescue or release; the psalm says Yahweh has sent redemption to his people.
